scene.e1.rests.1: A rest is a beat of silence. Keep counting while you wait.
scene.e1.rests.2: Play, rest, play, rest: one, two, three, four.
scene.e1.lh.1: Your left hand has numbers too: the thumb is 1, the little finger is 5.
scene.e1.lh.2: Little finger on the C below middle C. These notes live on the bass staff.
scene.e1.together.1: Both thumbs near middle C. The left hand holds a long note while the right hand moves.
scene.e1.eighths.1: Two eighth notes fit in one beat. Count: one-and, two-and.

scene.e3.lhg.1: Move your left hand down: little finger on the G below, thumb on D.
scene.e3.sharp.1: A sharp (♯) raises a note to the very next key on the right. F sharp is the black key just right of F.
scene.e3.flat.1: A flat (♭) lowers a note to the very next key on the left. B flat is the black key just left of B.
scene.e3.scale.1: Play C, D, E with fingers 1, 2, 3, then tuck your thumb under to play F and keep going up to C.

scene.c1.dotted.1: Baroque music, like Vivaldi's, loves a long-short lilt. A dotted quarter lasts as long as three eighths.
scene.c1.dotted.2: Hold the long note, then play the short one right before the next beat. Count: one-and-two-and.
scene.c1.pickup.1: Classical tunes, like Haydn's and Mozart's, often begin with a pickup: a short first bar that leads into the first strong beat.
scene.c1.pickup.2: Count the empty beats silently, then play the pickup on the last beat of the bar.
scene.c1.bass.1: In Baroque music the left hand often walks: it moves step by step under the tune, one finger per note.
scene.c1.bass.2: Later, play two notes together, a fifth or a sixth apart, for a fuller Romantic sound. Keep fingers 5 and 1 on the notes.
scene.c1.minor.1: Romantic composers love minor keys. In A minor the G is raised to G sharp, the black key just left of A.
scene.c1.minor.2: Play E, G sharp, A with fingers 3, 3, 4 and then slide down: finger 1 on G sharp leads to A.
scene.c1.reach.1: Romantic melodies climb high. Play C, D, E, G, then move your whole hand up so the thumb sits on G.
scene.c1.reach.2: From the new position, reach B, C and D with fingers 3, 4 and 5. Keep your wrist relaxed.

scene.i1.crossing.1: Going up with the right hand: after finger 3, tuck your thumb under to play F.
scene.i1.crossing.2: Left hand going up: cross finger 3 over your thumb to keep climbing.
scene.i1.dpos.1: D position: thumb on D, and F sharp (the black key) under finger 3.
scene.i1.twofour.1: In 2/4 time each bar has two beats: ONE, two. It feels like a march.
scene.i1.rhythm.1: Syncopation: a short note, a long note in the middle, then a short one. The long note lands between the beats.
scene.i1.rhythm.2: Dotted rhythm: hold the long note one and a half beats, then play the quick note right after it.
scene.i1.broken.1: Broken fifth: play the bottom note, then the top note, one after the other. Keep your hand relaxed.

scene.i3.aminor.1: A minor uses the white keys from A to A. Its seventh note, G, is often raised to G sharp to pull harder towards home.
scene.i3.aminor.2: Play A to E, then try E, F, G sharp, A.
scene.i3.chords.1: In C, the chords are I (C-E-G), IV (C-F-A) and V7 (B-F-G). Play each as a block first.
scene.i3.chords.2: Then break the chord: play its notes one at a time, low to high and back.
scene.i3.coord.1: Parallel motion: both hands travel the same way, finger for finger.
scene.i3.coord.2: Contrary motion: the hands move apart or together, like a mirror.
scene.i3.ext.1: Your five fingers can reach one key further. Stretch the little finger up to D without moving the whole hand.
scene.i3.ext.2: Reach, play, then let the hand follow the tune.
scene.i3.rag.1: Syncopation puts the accent between the beats. Short, long, short: the long note lands off the beat.
scene.i3.rag.2: Keep the left hand steady, like a ticking clock, while the right hand plays against it.

scene.b1.lh.1: Your right hand rests on D while the left hand takes the tune: little finger on G, then 4, 3 and thumb on D.
scene.b1.lh.2: Listen to the left hand as a singer. The right hand just holds the harmony.
scene.b1.imit.1: Imitation: the right hand plays a short tune.
scene.b1.imit.2: Now the left hand answers with the same tune, one octave lower.
scene.b1.seq.1: A sequence repeats a pattern starting on a new note. Play D, B, C, A.
scene.b1.seq.2: Now start one step lower: C, A, B, G. Same shape, new place.
scene.b1.mot.1: Parallel motion: both hands travel the same way, a tenth apart.
scene.b1.mot.2: Contrary motion: one hand goes up while the other goes down.
scene.b1.runs.1: Play a four-note run with the left hand, from G up to C.
scene.b1.runs.2: The right hand picks up the run exactly where the left hand stopped.

scene.b2.minor.1: In a minor key the seventh note is often raised by a half step. In D minor, C becomes C sharp.
scene.b2.minor.2: Listen to the pull: the raised note leans up into the home note.
scene.b2.phrase.1: A phrase is a musical sentence. Count four or eight bars and play them in one breath.
scene.b2.phrase.2: Shape the line: lean in toward the middle, then relax at the end.
scene.b2.sixteenth.1: Four sixteenth notes fit in one beat. Keep the left hand note held while the right hand runs.
scene.b2.sixteenth.2: Count 1-e-and-a and keep your fingers relaxed and close to the keys.
scene.b2.leap.1: Look at the target key before you jump: the left hand leaps an octave or a sixth.
scene.b2.leap.2: Keep your wrist loose and land softly on the new note.
scene.b2.susp.1: A suspension holds a note while the bass moves underneath it. It clashes for a moment.
scene.b2.susp.2: Then the held note steps down and resolves. Hold, listen, release.

scene.i2.shift.1: Play C, E, G. While the long G rings, slide your whole hand up to the G position.
scene.i2.shift.2: Move on a long note or a rest, so your next note lands without a hitch.
scene.i2.stretch.1: Keep your thumb on C and let your little finger reach up to A, B and C.
scene.i2.stretch.2: Stretch only your fingers. Keep your wrist relaxed and your hand quiet.
scene.i2.gmajor.1: G major has one sharp: every F becomes F sharp, the black key right of F.
scene.i2.gmajor.2: The sharp sits at the start of the staff, so it is not written again in every bar.
scene.i2.repeat.1: On a repeated note, change fingers each time: 3, 2, 1. The new finger gets the key ready.
scene.i2.repeat.2: Let your hand glide as the fingers change, so the repeats stay light and even.
scene.i2.octave.1: For an octave jump, put your little finger on the low note and your thumb on the high one.
scene.i2.octave.2: Look ahead to the next note, then jump with your arm, not just your fingers.

scene.i4.gscale.1: Play G A B with fingers 1, 2, 3, then tuck your thumb under to play C.
scene.i4.gscale.2: Keep going up to G, and watch for F sharp, the black key before the top note.
scene.i4.dmajor.1: D major has two sharps: F sharp and C sharp. Start with your thumb on D.
scene.i4.dmajor.2: Play the scale up to D, then use the same fingering as G major.
scene.i4.sixeight.1: In 6/8 you feel two big beats, and each beat splits into three eighth notes.
scene.i4.sixeight.2: A dotted quarter fills a whole beat: count one-two-three, four-five-six.
scene.i4.triplets.1: A triplet squeezes three even notes into one beat. Say tri-pl-et for each group.
scene.i4.triplets.2: Keep the beat steady: the triplet is faster than eighths, but the pulse never changes.
scene.i4.highc.1: From G, jump your whole hand up so your thumb lands on high C.
scene.i4.highc.2: Now your fingers rest on C, D, E, F, G. Look at the keys before you move.

scene.bc1.dom7.1: Add the flat seventh to a chord and it growls. C7 is C, E, G and B flat: play the shape with fingers 1, 3 and 5.
scene.bc1.dom7.2: F7 and G7 use the same hand shape, just one step higher each time. Slide your hand up with no big jumps.
scene.bc1.swing.1: In swing, pairs of eighth notes are uneven: the first is long, the second is short. Think of it as a bouncy long-short, long-short.
scene.bc1.shuffle.1: The shuffle bass climbs and falls: root, fifth, sixth, fifth. In C that is C, G, A, G. Move the same shape to F and G.
scene.bc1.boogie.1: Boogie walks: root, third, fifth, sixth, flat seventh, then back down. Eight even eighth notes in every bar, steady as a train.
scene.bc1.blues.1: The blues scale adds a gritty note: C, E flat, F, F sharp, G. Slide up it with fingers 1 to 5, then riff on it.

scene.ls1.lead.1: A lead sheet shows the tune plus a chord name above each bar. Your right hand plays the melody.
scene.ls1.lead.2: The letter tells your left hand what to play: C means a C chord.
scene.ls1.cg.1: C is C, E, G with fingers 5, 3, 1. Press all three keys together.
scene.ls1.cg.2: G7 is B, F, G: move your hand a step down and keep the same shape of fingers 5, 2, 1.
scene.ls1.f.1: Here is C again. Now slide your middle finger up to F and your thumb to A.
scene.ls1.f.2: F is C, F, A with fingers 5, 2, 1. C, F and G7 are the three chords of most songs.
scene.ls1.am.1: A minor is C, E, A. Keep your 5 and 3 where they are and only your thumb moves up to A.
scene.ls1.am.2: Compare it with F: only the middle finger changes. Am sounds softer and sadder.
scene.ls1.mid.1: Sometimes a bar holds two chords. Play the first on beats 1 and 2, then switch.
scene.ls1.mid.2: Look ahead: find the next chord shape before beat 3 so the change stays on time.

scene.pa2.triads.1: A triad stacks three notes: root, third and fifth. In the left hand use fingers 5, 3 and 1 on C, E and G.
scene.pa2.triads.2: Move the bottom note to the top and you get an inversion: same chord, new shape.
scene.pa2.oompah.1: Oom-pah: a low bass note on beats 1 and 3, a chord on beats 2 and 4.
scene.pa2.oompah.2: Keep the chord light and let the bass lead. Bounce your wrist between the two.
scene.pa2.waltz.1: Waltz bass in 3/4: ONE is a low note, then two soft chords on beats two and three.
scene.pa2.waltz.2: The chord stays put while the bass note changes with each new harmony.
scene.pa2.alberti.1: Alberti bass breaks a chord into low, high, middle, high. Fingers 5, 1, 3, 1.
scene.pa2.alberti.2: Repeat the pattern evenly, like a quiet motor under the melody.
scene.pa2.arp.1: An arpeggio rolls a chord up and down over an octave. Fingers 5, 3, 2, 1 going up.
scene.pa2.arp.2: Come back down smoothly and keep your wrist loose, travelling with the notes.

scene.pa1.keys.1: The key signature sits at the start of every line. It tells you which notes are always sharp or flat, so you do not need a sign on each one.
scene.pa1.keys.2: Two sharps, F and C, mean D major; one flat, B, means F major. Each step around the circle of fifths adds one sharp or one flat.
scene.pa1.keys.3: Before you play, read the signature and say the sharps or flats out loud.
scene.pa1.sixteenth.1: A sixteenth note is a quarter of a beat. Four of them fit in one beat, so they go twice as fast as eighths.
scene.pa1.sixteenth.2: Keep your fingers close to the keys and your hand loose. Count one-e-and-a for each beat.
scene.pa1.dotted.1: A dot adds half the note's value. A dotted eighth plus a sixteenth fill one beat: a long note, then a quick one.
scene.pa1.dotted.2: Hold the long note almost to the end of the beat, then play the short note just before the next one.
scene.pa1.chromatic.1: A chromatic line moves by half steps, using every white and black key in a row.
scene.pa1.chromatic.2: Use thumb and third finger on the way up, and reach the black keys with your longer fingers.
scene.pa1.chords.1: Play three notes together in the right hand: fingers one, three and five. In the left hand, play the same note an octave apart with five and one.
scene.pa1.chords.2: Drop all the fingers together with a relaxed wrist so the notes sound at the same moment.

scene.sl.read.1: A slash chord names the chord first and the bass note after the slash. C/E is a C chord with E in the bass.
scene.sl.inversion.1: Turn a chord around and its bottom note changes. C, C/E and C/G are the same chord with a different bass note.
scene.sl.pedal.1: A pedal bass stays on one note while the chords above change. Keep your left hand on C and let the right hand move.
scene.sl.descend.1: Slash chords let the bass walk down step by step: C, B, A, G, F, E. The chords above follow the line.
scene.sl.sus.1: Put F over a G bass and the sound hangs, waiting to resolve. Bb over C does the same. Then land on G or C.

scene.sct.turn.1: A turn circles a note with four quick sixteenths: B, A, G sharp, A. Then it lands on the next note.
scene.sct.turn.2: Keep the turn light and even, like a quick shiver, and never rush the note that follows.
scene.sct.octave.1: Broken octaves: the left hand hops between a low note and the same note one octave higher.
scene.sct.octave.2: Use finger 5 for the low note and finger 1 for the high one. Keep the wrist loose and bouncy.
scene.sct.thirds.1: Parallel thirds are two notes two steps apart that move together, like F sharp and A, then E and G.
scene.sct.thirds.2: Press both notes at exactly the same moment, using fingers 2 and 4, and keep the hand shape steady.
scene.sct.chords.1: In the refrain the right hand plays octaves: the same note twice, with fingers 5 and 1.
scene.sct.chords.2: Keep the span steady and move the whole hand as one block, with the beat on the left hand.
scene.sct.runs.1: Sixteenth runs go four notes to every beat. Here the hand rolls down from A to F sharp.
scene.sct.runs.2: Watch for the sharps, including E sharp, which is the same key as F. Stay relaxed and light.

scene.jc2.bm7b5.1: Bm7b5 stacks B, D, F and A. It is a minor chord with a flat fifth, called half-diminished.
scene.jc2.bm7b5.2: Your left hand plays D, F and A while the bass plays B. Listen to the dark, tense color.
scene.jc2.m251.1: A minor ii-V-i goes Bm7b5, then E7, then Am. The tension builds, then settles home.
scene.jc2.m251.2: Only one or two notes move from chord to chord. Keep your hand relaxed and close.
scene.jc2.dim7.1: A diminished 7th chord is built from stacked minor thirds. It slides between two chords like a passing step.
scene.jc2.dim7.2: Move up one half step: C, then C sharp diminished, then D minor 7.
scene.jc2.jwaltz.1: A jazz waltz counts ONE two three. Play the bass note, then the chord twice.
scene.jc2.jwaltz.2: Let the eighth notes swing: long, short, long, short.
scene.jc2.sixths.1: A 6th chord adds the sixth note of the scale to a major chord: C, E, G and A.
scene.jc2.sixths.2: A tag ending repeats the last two bars, then settles on a warm 6th chord.

scene.ls2.gchords.1: Each chord symbol over the music names a left-hand chord. Play it with fingers 5, 3 and 1. In the key of G you need G, C and D7.
scene.ls2.gchords.2: D7 adds a spicy note that pulls the music back home to G.
scene.ls2.minor.1: Em is a minor chord: its middle note sits a little lower, so it sounds softer and more serious.
scene.ls2.minor.2: Dm works the same way: D, F, A. Compare it with D major, which has F sharp in the middle.
scene.ls2.g7.1: G7 in root position stacks G, B and F. Use fingers 5, 3 and 1.
scene.ls2.g7.2: Start on B instead and you get the same G7 sound, but sitting right next to C. Smaller moves, smoother music.
scene.ls2.waltz.1: In a waltz the left hand plays a bass note on ONE, then a small chord on two and three: oom-pah-pah.
scene.ls2.keyf.1: In the key of F the main chords are F, Bb and C7. Bb uses the black key just left of B.

scene.pc3.d-major.1: D major is D, F sharp and A. In the key of D, your home chords are D, G and A.
scene.pc3.d-major.2: Slide your left hand to G, then to A. Keep the same relaxed hand shape.
scene.pc3.a-major.1: A major is A, C sharp and E. In the key of A, your home chords are A, D and E.
scene.pc3.a-major.2: E major has a G sharp: E, G sharp, B. It always wants to resolve back home to A.
scene.pc3.b-minor.1: B minor shares D and F sharp with D major. Only the bottom note changes, to B.
scene.pc3.b-minor.2: Play D, A, B minor, G in a loop. Four chords power countless songs.
scene.pc3.inversions.1: A chord keeps the same three notes, even when you shuffle their order. Root position has the chord's name note at the bottom.
scene.pc3.inversions.2: First inversion puts the middle note at the bottom, second inversion puts the top note there. Same chord, new shape.
scene.pc3.voice-leading.1: Start with C. Now pick the G shape closest to it: only two notes move, and one stays put.
scene.pc3.voice-leading.2: Keep choosing the nearest shape for each new chord. Your hand barely moves and the chords flow.

scene.cs1.broken.1: A broken chord plays a chord's notes one at a time. Right hand: thumb, middle, little finger, then back to the middle (1, 3, 5, 3).
scene.cs1.broken.2: In the left hand play root, fifth, octave, then the fifth again, with fingers 5, 2, 1, 2.
scene.cs1.split.1: Bass plus chord: play the low root note on the beat, then the whole chord above it. Bass, chord, bass, chord.
scene.cs1.amhome.1: A minor uses the same white keys as C major, but A is home. Four chords build the sound: Am, F, C and G.
scene.cs1.emajor.1: E major needs one black key: G sharp. Play E, G sharp and B together, then slide back home to A minor.
scene.cs1.sixeight.1: In 6/8 you feel two big beats of three: ONE two three, FOUR five six. Roll the left hand up the chord and back down.

scene.ar1.inversions.1: An inversion is the same chord with its notes in a new order. Play C as C-E-G, then E-G-C, then G-C-E: same sound, new shape under your hand.
scene.ar1.thumbunder.1: Play C, E, G with fingers 1, 2, 3, then tuck your thumb under to the next C and keep rolling up. Finish on finger 5.
scene.ar1.crossover.1: Coming down, use fingers 5, 3, 2, 1, then pass finger 3 over your thumb and keep rolling down. Keep your wrist loose.
scene.ar1.handtohand.1: The left hand starts the arpeggio and the right hand takes over, as if one hand played across both. Keep the rolling beat even at the hand change.
scene.ar1.prelude.1: Bach's Prelude repeats one small shape: a short rest, then three chord notes twice, over a steady left-hand pair. Keep the right hand even and the left hand quiet.

scene.jc1.voicings.1: A seventh chord has four notes. Dm7 is D, F, A and C: play it with fingers 1, 2, 3 and 5.
scene.jc1.voicings.2: Cmaj7 is C, E, G and B. Swap between the two chords and keep your hand relaxed.
scene.jc1.leading.1: In a ii-V-I the chords share notes. From Dm7 to G7, D and F stay put and only two fingers move.
scene.jc1.leading.2: Now G7 to Cmaj7: G and B stay, while D and F step down by one. Smooth!
scene.jc1.shells.1: A shell is just two notes: the root and the seventh. Left hand: little finger on the root, thumb on the seventh.
scene.jc1.shells.2: Swap the seventh for the third and you get the other shell. With the right hand on top, they make a full chord.
scene.jc1.comping.1: Comping means playing chords under a tune. Hit the chord on beats 2 and 4 and rest on 1 and 3.
scene.jc1.comping.2: The Charleston rhythm: a chord on beat 1, then a short one on the 'and' of 2. Then rest.
scene.jc1.turnaround.1: A turnaround brings you back to the start: Cmaj7, Am7, Dm7, G7. Each chord moves by only a step or two.
scene.jc1.turnaround.2: Keep your hand calm: one or two fingers move at a time, the rest stay put.

scene.pc2.fchord.1: In F, your left hand plays F, Bb and C. Keep the little finger low and the thumb on top.
scene.pc2.fchord.2: Add a B flat on top of the C chord and you get C7, a chord that pulls back home to F.
scene.pc2.dm.1: D minor is the ii chord in C: D, F, A. It sits right next to C and G, so your hand barely moves.
scene.pc2.dm.2: Dm to G to C is a classic pop move: it leads you home like a staircase.
scene.pc2.prog.1: A progression is a loop of chords. I-vi-ii-V is C, Am, Dm, G. Each chord shares notes with the next, so keep your fingers close.
scene.pc2.prog.2: Em and F give you a second loop: I-iii-IV-V is C, Em, F, G. Learn the shapes, then listen for the pattern.
scene.pc2.mel.1: Now the right hand sings the melody while the left hand holds the chords. Play the chord, then the tune on top.
scene.pc2.mel.2: Listen to the chord under each melody note. The melody can move fast while the chords stay calm.
scene.pc2.bcc.1: In 3/4 the left hand plays bass, chord, chord: ONE is a single low note, two and three are the chord above it.
scene.pc2.bcc.2: Lift your hand a little for each new bar and the waltz will sway: boom, chick, chick.

scene.sce.rag.1: Ragtime lives on syncopation. Play a short note, a longer one, then a short one again, all inside one beat.
scene.sce.rag.2: Keep a steady pulse in your head and let the middle note ring a little longer. Now you try.
scene.sce.stride.1: Stride is the heartbeat of ragtime: a low bass note, then a chord, then bass again, then a chord.
scene.sce.stride.2: Bass on the beat, chord in between. Keep it light and even, like a bouncing ball.
scene.sce.chords.1: Rag melodies often climb in thirds. Press two keys at once with fingers 1 and 3.
scene.sce.chords.2: Climb step by step, then add a black key for the chromatic climb: C, D, D sharp, E.
scene.sce.fkey.1: Part C moves to F major. Every B becomes B flat, the black key just left of B.
scene.sce.fkey.2: Keep the same hand shape and let the left hand follow the F, B flat and D minor chords.
scene.sce.tips.1: Before you play the whole piece, remember three things. First, keep the left hand steady like a metronome.
scene.sce.tips.2: Rag is playful, never rushed. Choose a relaxed tempo and let the syncopation swing.
scene.sce.tips.3: Take a small breath at the end of each section and look ahead to your next hand position.
scene.sce.tips.4: If you slip, keep going. A steady beat matters more than a perfect note.

scene.scm.triplets.1: A triplet fits three even notes into one beat. Say tri-pl-et as you play thumb, middle finger, little finger.
scene.scm.triplets.2: Keep every note soft and perfectly even, like gently rocking water.
scene.scm.octaves.1: Play the low note with your little finger and the note an octave higher with your thumb, together. Let your arm weight sink into the keys.
scene.scm.dotted.1: A dotted eighth plus a sixteenth sounds long-short. Hold the long note almost to the next beat, then flick the short one.
scene.scm.together.1: The left hand sinks into one octave while the right hand rocks through three notes on every beat. Count 1-2-3, 2-2-3, 3-2-3, 4-2-3.
scene.scm.together.2: When the bass changes, the right hand shifts its shape with it.
scene.scm.climb.1: Let your wrist roll gently upward as your fingers climb the arpeggio. Each group of three starts a little higher.

scene.pc1.triad.1: A triad is three notes a skip apart: root, third and fifth.
scene.pc1.triad.2: Press C, E and G together with fingers 1, 3 and 5.
scene.pc1.g.1: For G, play B, D and G: the thumb slides one key down, the top note stays.
scene.pc1.amf.1: Am is A, C, E. Keep your thumb on A.
scene.pc1.amf.2: For F, keep A and C and move the top finger up to F.
scene.pc1.bass.1: The left hand plays the chord's name note, low down, while the right hand plays the chord.
scene.pc1.symbols.1: Letters above the music are chord symbols: C means the C chord, Am means A minor.
scene.pc1.symbols.2: When the symbol changes, switch to the new shape.

scene.cs2.rock-bass.1: For a rock bass, play the root and the fifth of the chord in steady eighth notes with your left hand: 5, 1, 5, 1.
scene.cs2.pulse.1: Play the whole chord in steady eighth notes with your right hand. Keep your wrist loose and every hit the same size.
scene.cs2.push.1: A push plays the next chord an eighth note early, on the 'and' of 4. Play it, leave the next downbeat quiet, and let the chord ring.
scene.cs2.ballad.1: In a ballad the left hand plays slow octaves while the right hand breaks the chord into gentle eighth notes.
scene.cs2.top-note.1: Play the melody note as the top of a chord. Lean a little more weight on your fifth finger so the tune sings out.

scene.ls3.dkey.1: In D major, F and C are sharp. Play the D chord with fingers 5, 3, 1, then G (B, D, G).
scene.ls3.dkey.2: Next comes A (C sharp, E, A). A7 changes only one note: A drops to G.
scene.ls3.akey.1: In A major, F, C and G are sharp. Play A with fingers 5, 3, 1, then D (A, D, F sharp).
scene.ls3.akey.2: E7 uses G sharp, B and D. Every note slides one step to reach A again.
scene.ls3.bm.1: B minor shares notes with D: B, D, F sharp. Slide from D to Bm by moving only the low note.
scene.ls3.bm.2: Now the loop D, Bm, G, A: it fits hundreds of songs. Keep your hand close to the keys.
scene.ls3.broken.1: A broken chord plays the notes one at a time: root, fifth, octave, fifth. Count 1 and 2 and.
scene.ls3.broken.2: Another pattern: root, fifth, third, fifth. Stay inside one hand position and keep it even.
scene.ls3.third.1: On a long melody note you can add a harmony note a third below. Start with one finger on F sharp.
scene.ls3.third.2: Now add D under it with your thumb: fingers 1 and 3 together. Then slide up for F sharp and A.

scene.cs3.alt-bass.1: Alternating bass: play the root of the chord with finger 5, then the fifth above it with your thumb. Keep swinging between them: root, fifth, root, fifth.
scene.cs3.boom-chick.1: Boom-chick: your left hand plays the bass on beats 1 and 3, and your right hand plays the chord on beats 2 and 4. The hands take turns.
scene.cs3.waltz-style.1: Waltz style: a bass note on ONE, then a small chord on two and three. G7 and D7 each get their own shape, so watch where the fingers go.
scene.cs3.key-g.1: In the key of G the main chords are G, C, D and Em. D7 adds a C and pulls even harder back home to G.
scene.cs3.passing.1: A passing bass walks between chords. Over C, walk down C, B, A with your left hand and land on the Am chord.

scene.adv1.em.1: E minor: the left hand plays the same chord again and again, light and even, like a quiet heartbeat.
scene.adv1.em.2: Keep the chord soft and let the right hand sing above it. Lift only your wrist, never your whole arm.
scene.adv1.maz.1: Mazurka rhythm: a long-short pair, then two quarter notes. The long-short pair is a dotted eighth and a sixteenth.
scene.adv1.maz.2: Lean on the second beat. The left hand plays a low bass, then two lighter chords.
scene.adv1.wide.1: The left hand rolls a broken chord across a whole tenth: low root, fifth, octave, then the third above.
scene.adv1.wide.2: Rotate your forearm smoothly and let your thumb arrive early. Keep your shoulder relaxed.
scene.adv1.tri.1: Three against two: the right hand plays three notes in the time the left hand plays two.
scene.adv1.tri.2: Say 'tri-pu-let' for the right hand and count the left hand evenly in your head.
scene.adv1.orn.1: A grace note is a tiny note squeezed in right before the main note. Play it quickly and land on the main note.
scene.adv1.orn.2: A mordent: main note, the note below, then the main note again, all very fast.
scene.adv1.orn.3: A turn circles the main note: the note above, the main note, the note below, then the main note.
scene.adv1.orn.4: A short trill swaps the main note and the note above in 32nd notes. Stay close to the keys.
